The analogue of Theorem 1.1 is the following (we state it only for ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},\frac{1}{2})}$ as the Gaussian and spherical models coincide in the 1/2-density case).

#### Proposition 1.3.

Suppose that (A) holds and $H$ is connected. Then, there exists some absolute constant $C$ depending only on $\epsilon,\gamma$ in (A) such that for $\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},\frac{1}{2})},$

$$ \Big|\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-1/2)\Big]\Big|\leq(1/2)^{|E(H)|}\times\Big(\frac{C\times|V(H)|\times|E(H)|\times(\log d)^{3/2})}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)^{\mathsf{SOEI}(H)}. $$

If an edge $(uv)$ is strongly covered, then the connected component $F^{(\pi)}_{\geq v,\ni u}$ contains a neighbour of $u.$ Hence, there exists a fragile edge with endpoint $u$ and $u$ is also covered according to Definition 4. Thus, $\mathsf{SOEI}(H)\geq\mathsf{OEI}(H),$ so Proposition 1.3 is at least as strong as Theorem 1.1. It turns out that the inequality is strict for many sparse graphs. For example, one can check that when $H=C_{k}$ is a cycle, $\mathsf{OEI}(C_{k})=\lceil(k-1)/2\rceil,$ but $\mathsf{SOEI}(H)=k-2.$ The latter follows from the following bound:

#### Proposition 1.4 (Strong Edge Independence Number of Sparse Graphs).

Suppose that $H$ is connected. Then, $\mathsf{SOEI}(H)\geq 2|V(H)|-|E(H)|-2.$

It turns out that the $\mathsf{OEI}(H)$ bound is too weak for our results on the second eigenvalue of ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},\frac{1}{2})}$ and we need $\mathsf{SOEI}(H)$ and Proposition 1.4. We leave open the problem of proving Proposition 1.3 for all densities $p$ .

#### 1.4.2 Application I: Testing Between Spherical RGG and Erdős-Rényi

In the case of spherical random geometric graphs, we not only confirm that the signed triangle statistic is optimal among low-degree polynomial tests, but also show that this is the case even in the non-adaptive edge-query model recently introduced by [MVW24]. For a mask $\mathcal{M}\in\{0,1\}^{N\times N}$ and (adjacency) matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N},$ denote by $A\odot\mathcal{M}$ the $N\times N$ array in which $(A\odot\mathcal{M})_{ji}=A_{ji}$ whenever $\mathcal{M}_{ji}=1$ and $(A\odot\mathcal{M})_{ji}=?$ whenever $\mathcal{M}_{ji}=0.$

Testing between graph distributions with masks corresponds to a non-adaptive edge query model. Instead of viewing a full graph, one can choose to observe a smaller more structured set of edges in order to obtain a more data-efficient algorithm. This idea was introduced recently in [MVW24], focusing on the planted clique problem. We obtain the following result for $\mathsf{RGG}$ .

#### Theorem 1.5.

Consider some $M$ where $n\coloneqq\sqrt{M},d,p$ satisfy the assumptions in (A). Let $\mathcal{M}$ be any graph on $M$ edges without isolated vertices. Denote by $N$ the number of vertices in $\mathcal{M}$ . If $d\geq(M^{1/2}p)^{3+c}$ for any constant $c>0,$ no degree $(\log n)^{1.1}$ polynomial can distinguish with probability $\Omega(1)$ the distributions $\mathbf{G}_{0}\odot\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathbf{G}_{1}\odot\mathcal{M}$ for $\mathbf{G}_{0}\sim\mathsf{G}(N,p)$ and $\mathbf{G}_{1}\sim\mathsf{RGG}(N,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p).$

We prove Theorem 1.5 in Section 4 via a standard $\chi^{2}$ argument using the bounds on Fourier coefficients in Theorem 1.1. In the case $\mathcal{M}=K_{n},$ we match the conjectured information-theoretic threshold. Theorem 1.5 is tight in light of the signed triangle statistic [LMSY22].

#### Corollary 1.2.

Consider some $n,d,p$ satisfying assumptions in (A). If $d\geq(np)^{3+c}$ for any positive constant $c,$ no degree $(\log n)^{1.1}$ polynomial can distinguish with probability $\Omega(1),$ the distributions $\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ and ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}.$

#### 1.4.3 Application II: Testing Between Gaussian RGG and Erdős-Rényi

We begin with a brief comparison of the Gaussian and spherical models.

#### Remark 2 (Gaussian vs Spherical Random Geometric Graphs).

The Gaussian and spherical models coincide in the case $p=1/2.$ More generally, they are intimately related due to the facts

$$ \displaystyle\text{If }Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d}),\text{ then }V:=Z/\|Z\|_{2}\sim\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1}),\text{ and} \displaystyle\text{If }Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tfrac{1}{d}I_{d}),\text{ then }\|Z\|_{2}\approx 1\text{ with high probability}. $$

This correspondence has been used to argue about either model – in some arguments more helpful is independence of Gaussian coordinates [DGLU11, BDER14] while in others orthonormality of the Gegenbauer basis over the sphere [LS23]. We exploit this correspondence in both directions.

We also show that the two models are qualitatively different in the sparse regime (see Fig. 1). The cause of this difference is the perhaps benign looking fact that Eq. II is only an approximate statement. This creates dependence between edges in the Gaussian case for edges which are independent in the spherical case: For example, under $\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)},$ the edges $\mathbf{G}_{21}$ and $\mathbf{G}_{31}$ are independent. In contrast, under $\mathbf{H}\sim{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)},$ $\mathbf{H}_{21},\mathbf{H}_{31}$ are positively correlated as both are monotone in $\|Z_{1}\|_{2}.$ The dependence turns out to be quite strong for small values of $p$ to the point where (signed) wedges are better than signed triangles for testing against Erdős-Rényi.

#### Theorem 1.6.

Consider the task of testing between ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}$ and $\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ under (A).

- 1. When $d\geq\max\big\{(n^{3}p^{3})^{1+c},(n^{3/2}p)^{1+c}\big\}$ for any constant $c>0,$ no degree $(\log n)^{1.1}$ algorithm can distinguish the two graph models with probability $\Omega(1).$

- 2. When $d\leq n^{3/2}p(\log n)^{-5}$ and $p\leq 0.49,$ the signed wedge count succeeds w.h.p.

- 3. When $d\leq n^{3}p^{3}(\log n)^{-5},$ the signed triangle count succeeds w.h.p.

In the non-adaptive query complexity model, the difference turns out to be even more dramatic. One can exploit the fact that wedges are highly informative by querying a star-graph, as star graphs maximize the number of wedges for a fixed number of edges.

#### Theorem 1.7.

Consider some $M$ where $n\coloneqq\sqrt{M},d,p$ satisfy the assumptions in (A). Let $\mathcal{M}$ be any graph on $M$ edges with no isolated vertices. Let $N$ be the number of vertices in $\mathcal{M}$ . Consider testing between $\mathbf{G}_{0}\odot\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathbf{G}_{1}\odot\mathcal{M}$ for $\mathbf{G}_{0}\sim\mathsf{G}(N,p),\mathbf{G}_{1}\sim\mathsf{RGG}(N,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p).$

- 1. When $d\geq\max\big\{(M^{3/2}p^{3})^{1+c},(Mp)^{1+c}\big\}=\max\big\{(n^{3}p^{3})^{1+c},(n^{2}p)^{1+c}\big\}$ for any constant $c>0,$ no degree $(\log n)^{1.1}$ algorithm can distinguish the two graph models with probability $\Omega(1).$

- 2. When $d\leq Mp(\log M)^{-5}=\tilde{\Theta}(n^{2}p)$ and $p\leq 0.49,$ the signed wedge count succeeds w.h.p. One possible mask $\mathcal{M}$ is a union of $A=\lceil(\log M)^{17}\rceil$ disjoint stars with $\lfloor M/A\rfloor$ edges each.

- 3. When $d\leq(M^{3/2}p^{3})(\log M)^{-5}=\tilde{\Theta}(n^{3}p^{3}),$ the signed triangle count succeeds w.h.p. A possible mask is $\mathcal{M}=K_{n}.$

The main message of this subsection is that even though the Gaussian and spherical models are closely related and each useful for reasoning about the other, they are also fundamentally different.

The proofs are similar to the ones in Section 1.4.2 and are provided in Sections 5 and A. We need to take extra care of graphs with leaves (as their Fourier coefficients are non-zero, unlike in the spherical case), which is done in Section A.6.

#### Remark 3.

The work [BBH21b] studies the convergence of masked Wishart matrices to GOE (that is $\mathbf{A}_{ji}=\langle Z_{i},Z_{j}\rangle$ instead of $\mathbf{G}_{ji}=\mathds{1}[\langle Z_{i},Z_{j}\rangle\geq\rho^{p}_{d}].$ ) Of course, for $p=o(1)$ the $\mathsf{RGG}$ testing problem becomes very different from the Wishart versus GOE problem [BBN19, LMSY22].

#### 1.4.4 Application III: Testing Between Spherical RGG and Planted Coloring

In the regime $d\leq(np)^{3-c}$ , $\mathsf{RGG}$ is very different from Erdős-Rényi. But is it, perhaps, closely approximated by some other simple model? We show that, with respect to low-degree polynomial tests, $\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},1/2)$ is indistinguishable from a slight variation of the planted coloring distribution in [KVWX23]. We focus on the density 1/2 case, but our arguments can be easily extended (we only use Theorem 1.1, not Proposition 1.3).

#### Definition 6.

$\mathsf{PCol}(n,q)$ is the following distribution over $n$ vertex graphs. First, each node $i\in[n]$ independently receives a uniform label $x_{i}\in[q].$ Then, if $x_{i}=x_{j},$ nodes $i$ and $j$ are adjacent with probability $1.$ If $x_{i}\neq x_{j},$ nodes $i$ and $j$ are adjacent with probability $\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}.$

In comparison, [KVWX23] have $i$ and $j$ adjacent with probability $1/2$ when $x_{i}\neq x_{j}$ . Choosing a value of $q$ so that the signed triangle counts of ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},\frac{1}{2})}$ and $\mathsf{PCol}(n,q)$ (nearly) match, we prove the following fact in Sections 6 and B.

#### Theorem 1.8.

Suppose that $d\geq n^{8/3+c}$ for any constant $c>0.$ Then, there exists some $q\in\big[{d^{1/4}}/(\log d),{d^{1/4}}(\log d)\big]$ such that no $(\log n)^{1.1}$ -degree polynomial test distinguishes $\mathsf{PCol}(n,q)$ and $\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},1/2)$ with probability $\Omega(1)$ .

#### Remark 4.

The condition $q=\tilde{\Theta}(d^{1/4})$ establishes a statistical-computational gap when $d\leq n^{4-\kappa}$ for any constant $\kappa>0.$ An instance of $\mathsf{PCol}(n,q)$ has a clique of size $n/q=\tilde{\Omega}(nd^{-1/4})$ with probability 1. However, ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},\frac{1}{2})}$ does not contain a clique of size more than $3\log_{2}n$ with high probability under (A) by [DGLU11]. Perhaps surprisingly, our result holds in the exact same regime as the results of [KVWX23] for refuting $q$ -colarability. Namely, $q=\tilde{\Theta}(d^{1/4}),d\geq n^{8/3}$ is equivalent to $q=\tilde{\Omega}(n^{2/3}).$ Our contribution here is not the analysis, but the realisation that $\mathsf{RGG}$ is indistinguishable from $\mathsf{PCol}.$ We prove hardness for detecting $q$ -colarability against the natural $\mathsf{PCol}$ model and do not need to construct a more sophisticated “quiet distribution” as in [KVWX23].

#### Remark 5.

[CW+19] studies a similar question for Wishart matrices in the regime $d=o(n^{3})$ when Wishart and GOE are distinguishable. The authors obtain a sequence of phase transitions for the Wishart density. The approximating densities are defined in terms of an inverse Fourier transform and are not easily interpretable, in contrast to the simple $\mathsf{PCol}$ distribution.

#### 1.4.5 Application IV: The Second Eigenvalue of Spherical RGG

#### Theorem 1.9.

Suppose that $\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},1/2)$ (equivalently $\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),\frac{1}{2})}$ ).

- • If $d\leq n(\log n)^{8},$ then with high probability $|\lambda_{2}(\mathbf{G})|\leq n(\log n)^{10}/\sqrt{d}.$

- • If $d\geq n(\log n)^{8},$ then with high probability $|\lambda_{2}(\mathbf{G})|\leq(\log n)^{10}\sqrt{n}.$

Here, we need the strong bounds in Proposition 1.4 for sparse graphs. As these bounds provably do not hold for $\mathsf{OEI},$ more work is needed to extend to $p\neq 1/2.$ The proof is in Section 7.

## 2 Proving the Bounds on Fourier Coefficients

Here, we prove our bounds on Fourier coefficients of random geometric graphs by formalizing the argument in Section 2. Specifically, in Section 2.1, we prove Theorem 1.1. In Section 2.3, we modify the argument slightly to prove the stronger Proposition 1.3 in the density $1/2$ case. In Section 2.2 we prove the bounds on the edge independence numbers stated in Propositions 1.2 and 1.4.

### 2.1 The Main Argument in Theorem 1.1

Fix a connected graph $H$ on $k=|V(H)|$ vertices and $m=|E(H)|$ edges such that $Ckm(\log d)^{3/2}\leq\sqrt{d}.$ Let $\pi$ be any bijective labeling of its vertices by $[k].$ We will identify vertices by their labelling in $\pi$ and optimize over $\pi$ at the end. We prove Theorem 1.1 in the Gaussian setting and state the necessary modifications for the spherical setting at the end.

#### Step 1: High-Probability Bound on $\sum_{\ell<i}Z_{i\ell}Z_{j\ell}+Z_{ji}(Z_{ii}-1)$ .

Recall Eq. 3. As discussed, dependence between edges is due to the term

$$ \begin{split}Q^{\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d})}_{ji}(\{Z_{j\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq j},\{Z_{i\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq i})\coloneqq\sum_{\ell<i}Z_{i\ell}Z_{j\ell}+Z_{ji}(Z_{ii}-1).\end{split} $$

We bound the size of this term, along the way introducing notation that will be used later. Let

$$ [\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{U}}]=\Big[-C\sqrt{\frac{m\log d}{{d}}},C\sqrt{\frac{m\log d}{{d}}}\Big] $$

be the “reasonable interval” for each summand in Eq. 5: By Gaussian and $\chi^{2}$ -concentration (3.4 and 3.5) for any desired constant $C^{\prime}$ , there exists some absolute constant $C$ such that under (A) (which implies $\log 1/p=O(\log d)$ and $\log n=O(\log d)$ ) we have $\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[Z_{i\ell}\in[\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{U}}]]\geq 1-e^{-C^{\prime}m\log d}$ and the same for $(Z_{ii}-1)$ . Denote by

$$ \mathcal{RSC}:=\Big\{Z_{uv}\in[\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{U}}]\text{ and }(Z_{uu}-1)\in[\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{U}}]\;\text{ for all }1\leq u\leq v\leq k\Big\} $$

the “reasonable set of configurations”. By the union bound its complement has probability

$$ \begin{split}&\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[\mathcal{RSC}^{c}]\leq k^{2}e^{-C^{\prime}m\log d}\leq p^{m}d^{-m}.\end{split} $$

As $Q^{\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d})}_{ji}$ is a sum of at most $k$ terms of order $(C\sqrt{{m\log d}/{{d}}})^{2}$ under the high probability event $\mathcal{RSC}$ , we conclude that with probability at least $1-p^{m}d^{-m},$

$$ \Big|Q^{\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d})}_{ji}(\{Z_{j\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq j},\{Z_{i\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq i})\Big|\leq C^{2}{\frac{km\log d}{{d}}}=\Delta\quad\text{for all }(ji)\in E(H), $$

where we defined $\Delta\coloneqq C^{2}{\frac{km\log d}{{d}}}.$ We condition on $\mathcal{RSC}.$ Since $|\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-p)|<1$ a.s.,

$$ \begin{split}\Big|\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-p)\Big]\Big|&\leq\Big|\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-p)\Big|\mathcal{RSC}\Big]\Big|+\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[\mathcal{RSC}^{c}]\\
&\leq\Big|\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-p)\Big|\mathcal{RSC}\Big]\Big|+p^{m}d^{-m}.\end{split} $$

As $p^{m}d^{-m}=p^{|E(H)|}d^{-|E(H)|}\leq p^{|E(H)|}\sqrt{d}^{-\mathsf{OEI}(H)}$ , it remains only to bound the first term.

#### Step 2: Fragile Edges.

Observe that under the high probability event in Eq. 7, as long as $Z_{ji}\not\in\big[\rho^{p}_{d}-\Delta,\rho^{p}_{d}+\Delta\big],$ it is the case that

$$ \mathds{1}[\langle Z_{i},Z_{j}\rangle\geq\rho^{p}_{d}]=\mathds{1}[Z_{ji}+{Q}^{\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})}_{ji}\geq\rho^{p}_{d}]=\mathds{1}[Z_{ji}\geq\rho^{p}_{d}] $$

and variables $Z_{ji}$ are independent (even conditioned on $\mathcal{RSC}$ ). Thus, all edges besides the ones for which $Z_{ji}$ is close to $\rho^{p}_{d}$ are independent. We localize dependence to the following fragile edges.

#### Definition 7 (Fragile Interval and Fragile Edges).

Denote $\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{L}}=\rho^{p}_{d}-\Delta$ and $\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{U}}=\rho^{p}_{d}+\Delta.$ The fragile interval is $[\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{U}}]$ and an edge $ji$ is called fragile if $Z_{ji}\in[\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{U}}].$

Note that each edge is fragile independently as $\{Z_{uv}\}_{1\leq u\leq v\leq k}$ are independent. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of fragile edges. Now, $Z_{ji}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1/d)$ and $\Delta=C^{2}{\frac{km\log d}{{d}}}=o(1/\sqrt{d})=o(\rho^{p}_{d}/\log d)$ imply

$$ \,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}\Big[Z_{ji}\in[\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{U}}]\Big]\leq\Delta p\sqrt{C^{\prime\prime}d\log d} $$

for some absolute constant $C^{\prime\prime}$ , because $[\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{U}}]$ has length $\Delta$ and the Gaussian density around $\rho^{p}_{d}$ is $\tilde{O}(p\sqrt{d})$ as $p=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[\langle Z_{1},Z_{2}\rangle\geq\rho^{p}_{d}]=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[Z_{11}Z_{21}\geq\rho^{p}_{d}]\approx\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[Z_{21}\geq\rho^{p}_{d}]$ and $Z_{21}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1/d).$ This is formalized via Corollary 3.5. Conditioning on the fragile set yields

$$ \begin{split}&\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-p)\Big|\mathcal{RSC}\Big]\\
&=\sum_{F\subseteq E(H)}\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-p)\Big|\mathcal{RSC},\mathcal{F}=F\Big]\times\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[\mathcal{F}=F|\mathcal{RSC}]\\
&\leq 2\sum_{F\subseteq E(H)}\Big|\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-p)\Big|\mathcal{RSC},\mathcal{F}=F\Big]\Big|\times\big(\Delta p\sqrt{C^{\prime\prime}d\log d}\big)^{|F|}.\end{split} $$

We used the fact that $\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[\mathcal{RSC}]\geq 1/2$ so $\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[\mathcal{F}=F|\mathcal{RSC}]\leq 2\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[\mathcal{F}=F].$ This last conditioning is useful, because our noise operator depends on the set of fragile edges.

#### Step 3: The noise operator.

Conditioned on the reasonable event $\mathcal{RSC}$ and on the set of fragile edges $\mathcal{F}=F,$ we define the following noise operator. It rerandomizes all variables $Z_{uv}$ such that the value of $Z_{uv}$ does not appear in the expression ${Q}^{\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})}_{ji}$ for any fragile $(ji)\in F.$ In particular, as ${Q}^{\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})}_{ji}$ is only a function of $\{Z_{j\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq j},\{Z_{i\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq i},$ we rerandomize all $(uv)\in E(H)\backslash(F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F)).$ For $(uv)\in E(H)\backslash(F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F)),$ conditioned on $\mathcal{RSC}$ and $\mathcal{F}=F,$ the variable $Z_{uv}$ uniquely determines $G_{uv}$ (as $(uv)$ is not fragile). Furthermore, $Z_{(uv)}$ is independent of $(G_{ji})_{(ji)\in E(H)\backslash\{(uv)\}}$ (as there is no fragile edge of the form $(ji)$ for which $(uv)\in\{{j\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq j}\cup\{{i\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq i}$ ). For clarity and uniformity with Observation 1.1, we spell this out separately.

#### Observation 2.1 (Noise Operator View on $\mathsf{RGG}$ ).

The noise operator $T_{p}^{\pi}$ on the distribution ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}$ is parametrized by an ordering of the vertices $\pi$ and marginal edge probability $p.$ To sample from $\mathsf{RGG},$ one first samples a fragile set $\mathcal{F}$ by including each edge independently with probability $\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[Z_{ji}\in[\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{U}}]]$ (recall that edges are fragile independently). $\mathcal{F}$ together with $\pi$ determines $\partial_{H}^{\pi}\mathcal{F}.$ Then, one samples $H_{\mathcal{F}\cup\partial_{H}^{\pi}\mathcal{F}}$ from the marginal distribution on edges $\mathcal{F}\cup\partial_{H}^{\pi}\mathcal{F}$ from the distribution ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}$ conditioned on $\mathcal{F}$ being the fragile set with respect to $\pi.$ Conditioned on $\mathcal{F},H_{\mathcal{F}\cup\partial_{H}^{\pi}\mathcal{F}},$ $T_{p}^{\pi}$ acts independently on edges with the following noise rates:

$$ \displaystyle T_{p}^{\pi}(G)_{uv}=\begin{cases}H_{uv}\;\text{ for }(uv)\in\mathcal{F}\cup\partial_{H}^{\pi}\mathcal{F}\text{ (case of no noise)},\\
\mathsf{Bern}(p)\;\text{ otherwise (case of full noise).}\end{cases} $$

That is, there is no noise on the edges in $\mathcal{F}\cup\partial\mathcal{F}$ and the rest of the edges are fully rerandomized. Hence, $T_{p}^{\pi}(\delta_{K_{n}})$ is a sample from ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}.$

One key difference with Observation 1.1 is that the distribution of the edge set $H_{\mathcal{F}\cup\partial^{\pi}\mathcal{F}}$ is much more complicated than the distribution on the planted clique $A.$ The latter is simply a clique, while $H_{\mathcal{F}\cup\partial_{H}^{\pi}\mathcal{F}}$ is a subgraph of a random geometric graph which is further conditioned on its fragile set.

Nevertheless, just as in Observation 1.1, the independent rerandomization over the rest of the edges $(\mathcal{F}\cup\partial_{H}^{\pi}\mathcal{F})^{c}$ yields an (exponentially fast) decay of Fourier coefficients, which we discuss next.

We separate the conditional signed expectation into the portion rerandomized by the noise operator, i.e. $E(H)\backslash(F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F)),$ and a portion that is not rerandomized, i.e. $F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F)$ :

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-p)\Big|\mathcal{RSC},\mathcal{F}=F\Big]\Big| \displaystyle=\Big|\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)\backslash(F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F))}\E\Big[(G_{ji}-p)\Big|\mathcal{RSC},\mathcal{F}=F\Big]\times\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F)}(G_{ji}-p)\Big|\mathcal{RSC},\mathcal{F}=F\Big]\Big| \displaystyle\leq\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)\backslash(F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F))}\Big|\E\Big[\mathds{1}[Z_{ji}\geq\rho^{p}_{d}]-p\Big|Z_{ji}\in[\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{U}}]\backslash[\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{U}}]\Big]\Big| \displaystyle\quad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\times\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F)}|G_{ji}-p|\;\Big|\mathcal{RSC},\mathcal{F}=F\Big]. $$

Next, we bound the factors for $E(H)\backslash(F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F))$ and then the factors for $F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F)$ .

#### Step 4: Factors $E(H)\backslash(F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H})$ Rerandomized By The Noise Operator.

A simple calculation with 1-dimensional Gaussian variables using Eqs. 6 and 9 and the fact that $\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[Z_{ji}\geq\rho^{p}_{d}]=p+O(p(\log d)/\sqrt{d})$ (see Corollary 3.5) gives

$$ \Big|\E\Big[\mathds{1}[Z_{ji}\geq\rho^{p}_{d}]-p\Big|Z_{ji}\in[\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{U}}]\backslash[\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{U}}]\Big]\Big|\leq\Delta p\sqrt{C^{\prime\prime\prime}d\log d}. $$

#### Step 5: Factors $F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}F$ .

Convexity of $|\cdot|,$ the fact $G_{ji}\leq 1$ a.s., and triangle inequality give

$$ \displaystyle\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F)}\big|G_{ji}-p\big|\;\Big|\mathcal{RSC},\mathcal{F}=F\Big] \displaystyle\leq\sum_{B\subseteq F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F)}p^{|F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F)|-|B|}\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in B}G_{ji}\;\Big|\;\mathcal{RSC},\mathcal{F}=F\Big] \displaystyle\leq\sum_{B\subseteq F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F)}p^{|F|+|\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F)|-|B|}\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in B\backslash F}G_{ji}\;\Big|\;\mathcal{RSC},\mathcal{F}=F\Big]. $$

For each $(ji)\in B\backslash F,$ the edge $G_{ji}$ is determined by $Z_{ji},$ conditioned on $\mathcal{RSC},\mathcal{F}=F.$ Thus,

$$ \E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in B\backslash F}G_{ji}\;\Big|\;\mathcal{RSC},\mathcal{F}=F\Big]=\E\big[\mathds{1}[Z_{ji}\geq\rho^{p}_{d}]|\mathcal{RSC},\mathcal{F}=F\big]^{|B|-|F|}. $$

By Eq. 12, the last expression is at most $(2p)^{|B|-|F|}.$ Plugging this into Eq. 13,

$$ \displaystyle\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F)}\big|G_{ji}-p\big|\;\Big|\mathcal{RSC},\mathcal{F}=F\Big] \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\leq\sum_{B\subseteq F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F)}p^{|F|+|\partial^{\pi}_{H}(F)|-|B|}\times(2p)^{|B|-|F|}\leq 4^{|E(H)|}(2p)^{|\partial^{\pi}_{H}F|}. $$

#### Step 6: Putting It All Together.

Plugging Eq. 12 and Eq. 14 into Eq. 11, the conditional Fourier coefficients are bounded as

$$ \begin{split}\Big|\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-p)\Big|\mathcal{RSC},\mathcal{F}=F\Big]\Big|\leq\big(\Delta p\sqrt{C^{\prime\prime\prime}d\log d}\big)^{|E(H)|-|F|-|\partial^{\pi}_{H}F|}\times 4^{|E(H)|}\times(2p)^{|\partial^{\pi}_{H}F|}.\end{split} $$

We combine this with Eq. 10 to obtain

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-p)\Big|\mathcal{RSC}\Big]\Big| \displaystyle\leq 2\sum_{F\subseteq E(H)}\big(\Delta p\sqrt{C^{\prime\prime}d\log d}\big)^{|E(H)|-|F|-|\partial^{\pi}_{H}F|}\times 4^{|E(H)|}\times(2p)^{|\partial^{\pi}_{H}F|}\times\big(\Delta p\sqrt{C^{\prime\prime\prime}d\log d}\big)^{|F|} \displaystyle\leq\max_{F\subseteq E(H)}2(8p)^{|E(H)|}\big(\Delta\sqrt{Cd\log d}\big)^{|E(H)|-|\partial^{\pi}_{H}F|}\leq\max_{F\subseteq E(H)}2(8p)^{|E(H)|}\Big(\frac{Ckm(\log d)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)^{|E(H)|-|\partial^{\pi}_{H}F|}. $$

All that is left to show is $|E(H)|-|\partial^{\pi}_{H}F|\geq\mathsf{OEI}_{\pi}(H).$ This follows immediately because for any $F\subseteq E(H),$ the set $E(H)\backslash\partial^{\pi}_{H}F$ satisfies the covering properties Definition 2 (note that $F\subseteq E(H)\backslash\partial^{\pi}_{H}F$ ). Finally, we can choose $\pi$ as the maximizer of $\mathsf{OEI}_{\pi}(H)$ and conclude Theorem 1.1 in the Gaussian case.

#### Remark 6 (Energy-Entropy Trade-off).

$|E(H)|-|\partial^{\pi}_{H}F|\geq\mathsf{OEI}_{\pi}(H)$ highlights the following energy-entropy trade-off phenomenon in $\mathsf{RGG}.$ Rewrite it as $|F|+|E(H)\backslash(F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}F)|\geq\mathsf{OEI}_{\pi}(H).$ The term $|E(H)\backslash(F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}F)|$ corresponds to entropy in the distribution as it is the size of the subset of edges which the noise operator rerandomizes (and are independent with all edges in $E(H)$ ). The term $|F|$ measures energy as $\mathcal{F}=F$ is the subset of edges with non-trivial interactions (dependence) with other edges in $|E(H)|.$ The inequality shows that energy and entropy cannot both be small, and either one being large results in small Fourier coefficient: entropy due to randomness and energy due to low probabilities.

#### The Spherical Case.

The analysis of the spherical case is nearly the same. We generate $V_{1},V_{2},\ldots,V_{k}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$ as $V_{i}=Z_{i}/\|Z_{i}\|_{2},$ where $Z_{1},Z_{2},\ldots,Z_{k}\sim_{iid}\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}).$ Then, we apply the Gram-Schmidt process on $Z_{1},Z_{2},\ldots,Z_{k}.$ With respect to the Bartlett decomposition,

$$ \langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle=\frac{1}{\|Z_{i}\|_{2}\times\|Z_{j}\|_{2}}\langle Z_{i},Z_{j}\rangle=Z_{ji}+{Q}^{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}_{(ji)}(\{Z_{j\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq j},\{Z_{i\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq i})\,, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle{Q}^{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}_{(ji)}(\{Z_{j\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq j},\{Z_{i\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq i}) \displaystyle\qquad\coloneqq\Big(\sum_{\ell<i}Z_{i\ell}Z_{j\ell}+Z_{ji}(Z_{ii}-1)\Big)\frac{1}{\|Z_{i}\|_{2}\times\|Z_{j}\|_{2}}+Z_{ji}\times\Big(\frac{1}{\|Z_{i}\|_{2}\times\|Z_{j}\|_{2}}-1\Big). $$

The function ${Q}^{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}_{(ji)}$ depends on the exact same set of variables as $Q^{\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d})}_{ji}$ and also takes value in $[-C^{\prime\prime\prime}pmk\log d/\sqrt{d},C^{\prime\prime\prime}pmk\log d/\sqrt{d}]$ under $\mathcal{RSC}.$ The rest of the analysis is identical.

### 2.2 Bounds on the Ordered Edge Independence Numbers.

#### Proof of first part of Proposition 1.2.

We first bound $\mathsf{OEI}_{\pi}(H)$ by another quantity. Denote by $\mathcal{SN}_{\pi}(H)$ the set of vertices $j$ of $H$ for which there exists some $i<j$ such that $(ji)\in E(H),$ i.e. with a smaller neighbour. Then, $\mathsf{OEI}_{\mathcal{A}}(H)\geq\lceil|\mathcal{SN}_{\pi}(H)|/2\rceil.$ To prove this, suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there exists a set of $r<|\mathcal{SN}_{\pi}(H)|/2$ edges $(j_{1},i_{1}),(j_{2},i_{2}),\ldots,(j_{r},i_{r})$ that satisfy the covering properties from Definition 2. Since $r<|\mathcal{SN}_{\pi}(H)|/2,$ $\Big|\{j_{1},i_{1},j_{2},i_{2},\ldots,j_{r},i_{r}\}\Big|<|\mathcal{SN}_{\pi}(H)|.$ Thus, there exists some vertex $j^{*}\in\mathcal{SN}_{\pi}(H)$ such that $j^{*}\not\in\{j_{1},i_{1},j_{2},i_{2},\ldots,j_{r},i_{r}\}.$ Let $i^{*}<j^{*}$ be a vertex such that $(j^{*}i^{*})$ is an edge. Such an $i^{*}$ exists by the definition of $\mathcal{SN}_{\pi}(H).$ But then, clearly, $(j^{*}i^{*})\not\in\partial^{\pi}_{H}F.$ This contradicts the fact that the edges $(j_{1},i_{1}),(j_{2},i_{2}),\ldots,(j_{r},i_{r})$ satisfy the covering properties.

Now, we need to show that $\max_{\pi}|\mathcal{SN}_{\pi}(H)|\geq|V(H)|-1$ for connected $H.$ Let $T$ be a rooted spanning tree of $H.$ Define $\pi$ to be any labelling of $H,$ such that for all $i,$ all vertices on level $i+1$ have a larger label than the vertices on level $i.$ Clearly, the root is the only vertex without a neighbour with a smaller label. ∎

#### Proof of second part of Proposition 1.2.

Recall that $\delta(H):=\max_{S\subseteq V(H)}\{|S|-|N_{H}(S)|\},$ where $N_{H}(S):=\{j\in V(H)\;:\;\exists i\in S\text{ s.t. }(ji)\in E(H)\}$ The inequality $\mathsf{OEI}(H)\geq\delta(H)+1$ is clear if $\delta(H)=0,$ so we assume throughout that $\delta(H)\geq 1.$ We need the following fact which we prove for completeness.

#### Proposition 2.1 ([Alo81]).

There exists an independent set $S^{\prime}\in\arg\max_{S}\{|S|-|N_{H}(S)|\}.$

#### Proof.

Take any $S^{\prime\prime}\in\arg\max_{S}\{|S|-|N_{H}(S)|\}.$ Then, $S^{\prime}=S^{\prime\prime}\backslash N(S^{\prime\prime})$ is an independent set and satisfies $|S^{\prime}|-|N_{H}(S^{\prime})|\geq|S^{\prime\prime}|-|N_{H}(S^{\prime\prime})|.$ ∎

Let $S^{\prime}\in\arg\max_{S}{|S|-|N_{H}(S)|}$ be independent and $N_{H}(S^{\prime})=\{u_{1},u_{2},\ldots,u_{\ell}\}.$ Define the sets

- 1. $S^{\prime}_{1}=N_{H}(u_{1})\cap S^{\prime}$ and

- 2. $S^{\prime}_{i}=\big(N_{H}(u_{i})\backslash(N_{H}(u_{1})\cup N_{H}(u_{2})\cup\cdots\cup N_{H}(u_{i-1}))\big)\cap S^{\prime}.$

Take any ordering $\pi$ such that the following vertices appear in the following decreasing order:

$$ S_{1}^{\prime},u_{1},S_{2}^{\prime},u_{2},\ldots,S_{\ell}^{\prime},u_{\ell},V(H)\backslash(S^{\prime}\cup N_{H}(S^{\prime})), $$

i.e. $\pi(x)>\pi(u_{1})$ for all $x\in S_{1}^{\prime},$ $\pi(u_{1})>\pi(y)$ for all $y\in S_{2}^{\prime},$ and so on. Let $F$ be any set satisfying the covering properties in Definition 2 with respect to this ordering. Observe that for each $k\in[\ell],v\in S^{\prime}_{k},$ the vertex $u_{k}$ is the only neighbour of $v$ among $S_{1}^{\prime}\cup S_{2}^{\prime}\cdots\cup S^{\prime}_{k}\cup\{u_{1},u_{2},\ldots,u_{k}\}.$ Thus, the set $F$ must include the edge $(vu_{k})$ as otherwise $(vu_{k})\not\in\partial^{\pi}_{H}F.$ As this holds for each $k\in[\ell],v\in S^{\prime}_{k},$ there are at least $\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}|S^{\prime}_{k}|=|S^{\prime}|=\delta(H)+|N(S^{\prime})|\geq\delta(H)+1$ edges in $F.$ ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 1.4.

Suppose that there exists a set $F$ satisfying the strong covering property for which $|F|<2|V(H)|-|E(H)|-2.$ In particular, the graph defined by vertices $V(H)$ and edges $F$ has $t>|V(H)|-(2|V(H)|-|E(H)|-2)=|E(H)|+2-|V(H)|$ connected components. Let $C_{1},C_{2},\ldots,C_{t}$ be these connected components. Since $H$ is connected, there exist at least $t-1$ pairs of different connected components $C_{i},C_{j}$ with an edge between them. However, if $(uv)$ is such an edge between different connected components, where $u\in C_{i},v\in C_{j}$ and $u>v,$ $v$ must have another neighbour in $C_{i}$ as $F$ satisfies the strong covering property in Definition 4. Thus, whenever there is an edge between $C_{i}$ and $C_{j},$ there are at least two such edges. Hence, the total number of edges in $H$ is at least

$$ 2(t-1)+\sum_{i=1}^{t}(|V(C_{i})|-1)=|V(H)|-t+2t-2=|V(H)|+t-2>|E(H)|, $$

which is a contradiction. ∎

#### Remark 7.

This proof holds for any ordering $\pi.$ We expect that choosing an optimal $\pi$ will yield an improved bound.

### 2.3 Improving The Bound in The Half-Density Case in Proposition 1.3

The density $1/2$ case is special as there is a measure preserving map between $[\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{L}}]$ and $[\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{U}},\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{U}}]$ which also preserves norms – namely, $\Xi(Z),$ where $\Xi(Z):=-Z.$ In particular, the analogue of Eq. 12 is

$$ \E\Big[\mathds{1}[Z_{ji}\geq\rho^{1/2}_{d}]-1/2\Big|Z_{ji}\in[\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{U}}]\backslash[\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{U}}]\Big]=0. $$

Thus, unless $(F\cup\partial^{\pi}_{H}F)=\emptyset,$ the expression in Eq. 11 is equal to 0. This immediately yields an improved bound on the Fourier coefficient of the form $2\times p^{|E(H)|}\times(C^{\prime\prime\prime}pkm(\log d)^{3/2}/\sqrt{d})^{\mathsf{OEI}(H)}.$

#### A more powerful noise operator.

The map $\Xi(Z),$ however, allows us to do more. One can apply a noise operator on certain edges adjacent to fragile edges. The reason is that

$$ Q^{\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d})}_{ji}(\{Z_{j\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq j},\{Z_{i\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq i})=Q^{\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d})}_{ji}(\{\Xi(Z_{j\ell})\}_{1\leq\ell\leq j,i\neq j},\{\Xi(Z_{i\ell})\}_{1\leq\ell<i},Z_{ii},Z_{ji}) $$

and similarly for the spherical analogue $Q^{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}_{ji}.$

Namely, condition on $\mathcal{F}=F.$ Take any $(ji)\in E(H)\backslash F$ such that, furthermore, $j$ is the unique neighbour of $i$ according to $H$ in $V(F^{\pi}_{\geq i,\ni j})$ (equivalently, $(ji)\in E(H)\backslash(F\cup\overline{\partial}^{\,\pi}_{H}F)$ by Definition 4). This means that the operation $(Z_{ai})_{a\in V(F^{\pi}_{\geq i,\ni j})}\longrightarrow(\Xi(Z_{ai}))_{a\in V(F^{\pi}_{\geq i,\ni j})}$ changes $G_{ji}$ to $1-G_{ji}$ but leaves all other edges $G_{uv}$ unchanged. Indeed, consider the cases for $(uv)$ :

- 1. $(uv)=(ja)$ for some $a\in V(F^{\pi}_{\geq i,\ni j}).$ However, $(ji)$ is the unique edge with this property.

- 2. $(uv)$ is not fragile and not of the form $(ja)$ for some $a\in V(F^{\pi}_{\geq i,\ni j}).$ Then, $Z_{uv}$ remains unchanged and so does $G_{uv}$ as $uv$ is not fragile.

- 3. $(uv)$ is fragile and at least one of $u$ and $v$ is not in $V(F^{\pi}_{\geq i,\ni j}).$ Then, either $\min(u,v)\leq i,$ in which case $G_{uv}$ can only depend on $Z_{ai}$ via its norm, $Z_{ai}^{2}$ (this follows from the definitions of ${Q}^{\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d})}_{uv}$ and ${Q}^{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}_{uv}$ ). However, $Z_{ai}^{2}=\Xi(Z_{ai})^{2}.$

- 4. $(uv)$ is fragile and $u,v\in V(F^{\pi}_{\geq i,\ni j}),$ in which case $G_{uv}$ depends on terms of the form $Z_{ai}$ via the product $Z_{ui}Z_{vi},$ but $Z_{ui}Z_{vi}=\Xi(Z_{ui})\Xi(Z_{vi})$ (again, this follows from the definitions of ${Q}^{\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d})}_{uv}$ and ${Q}^{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}_{uv}$ ).

With this property in mind, we define the following noise operator: for each edge $(ji)\in E(H)\backslash(F\cup\overline{\partial}^{\,\pi}_{H}F),$ one independently applies with probability $1/2$ the operation $(Z_{ai})_{a\in V(F^{\pi}_{\geq i,\ni j})}\longrightarrow(\Xi(Z_{ai}))_{a\in V(F^{\pi}_{\geq i,\ni j})}.$ As long as there is at least one such edge, the corresponding expected signed weight $\mathsf{SW}_{H}^{1/2}$ becomes zero.

By Definition 4, this is always the case if $|F|<\mathsf{SOEI}_{\pi}(H).$ An analogous argument to the one in Section 2.1 allows us to bound

$$ \Big|\E\Big[\prod_{ji\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-1/2)\Big]\Big|\leq 2\times p^{|E(H)|}\times(C^{\prime\prime\prime}pkm(\log d)^{3/2}/\sqrt{d})^{\mathsf{SOEI}_{\pi}(H)}. $$

Optimizing over the labelling $\pi$ yields Proposition 1.3.

#### Remark 8 (Why not other densities?).

In principle, we could have carried out the same argument for other densities by fixing some measurable bijection $\Xi_{p}:[\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{L}}]\longrightarrow[\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{U}},\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{U}}],\Xi_{p}:[\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{L}}]\longrightarrow[\mathsf{F}_{\mathsf{L}},\mathsf{R}_{\mathsf{L}}].$ Then, we apply it independently to variables $(Z_{ai})_{a\in V(F^{\pi}_{\geq i,\ni j})}$ for edges $(ji)\in E(H)\backslash(F\cup\overline{\partial}^{\,\pi}_{H}F)$ with some probability $\tilde{p}$ so that marginal distributions remain Gaussian. The difficulty with this approach is that for essentially any other density besides $1/2,$ the equality $Z_{ui}Z_{vi}=\Xi_{p}(Z_{ui})\Xi_{p}(Z_{vi})$ will not hold. Thus, the values of ${Q}^{\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d})}$ (resp, ${Q}^{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}$ ) will change and so it is not clear how fragile edges are affected by the respective noise operator.

## 3 Preliminaries

### 3.1 Graph Notation

Our graph notation is mostly standard. We denote by $V(H),E(H)$ the vertex and edge sets of a graph. For $i\in V(H),$ we define $N_{H}(i):=\{j\in V(H)\;:\;(ji)\in E(H)\}$ and for $S\subseteq V(H),$ $N_{H}(S):=\cup_{i\in S}N_{H}(i).$ $\delta(H):=\max_{S\subseteq V(H)}|S|-|\{j\in V(H)\;:\;\exists i\in S\text{ s.t. }(ji)\in E(H)\}|.$ Denote by $\mathsf{CC}(H)$ the set of connected components of $H.$ We denote by $K_{n}$ the complete graph on $n$ vertices, and by $\mathsf{Star}_{n}$ the star graph which has one central vertex $v$ and $n$ leaves $i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{n}$ adjacent to $v.$

We will frequently define graphs by the edges that induce them. That is, for $A\subseteq E(K_{n}),$ we also denote by $A$ the graph on vertex set $\{i\in V(K_{n})\;:\;\exists j\in V(K_{n})\text{ s.t. }(ji)\in A\}$ and edge set $A.$ Identifying graphs by edges that span them is convenient as edges are the variables of polynomials that we consider.

We define by $\mathcal{G}_{D}$ the set of graphs (up to isomorphism) on at least 1 edge and at most $D$ edges and by $\mathcal{NLG}_{D}\subseteq\mathcal{G}_{D}$ the subset of those graphs with no leaves.

### 3.2 Low-Degree Polynomials

Our results in Sections 1.4.2, 1.4.3 and 1.4.4 are based on the low-degree polynomial framework introduced in [HS17, Hop18]. One way to motivate it is the following. When testing between graph distributions $H_{0}$ and $H_{1}$ (say, $H_{0}=\mathsf{G}(n,p),H_{1}={\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}$ ), one observes a single graph $\mathbf{G}$ and needs to output 0 or 1. The graph $\mathbf{G}$ is simply a bit sequence in $\{0,1\}^{E(K_{n})}.$ Hence, the output is a function $f:\{0,1\}^{E(K_{n})}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}.$ All Boolean functions are polynomials [O’D14]. Therefore, one simply needs to compute a polynomial in the edges. Importantly, one can write polynomials over $\{0,1\}^{m}$ in their Fourier expansion. In the $p$ -biased case over graphs, one represents $f:\{0,1\}^{E(K_{n})}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ as

$$ f(G)=\sum_{H\;:\;H\subseteq E(K_{n})}\widehat{f}(H)\times(\sqrt{p(1-p)})^{-|E(H)|}\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-p). $$

Here, $\widehat{f}(H)$ is just a constant (the Fourier coefficient corresponding to $H$ ) and $\Big\{\sqrt{p(1-p)}^{-|E(H)|}\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-p)\Big\}_{H\subseteq E(K_{n})}$ is a basis of polynomials. Conveniently, as can be seen from Eq. 1, this basis is composed of signed-subgraphs $\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{H}.$ What makes it useful is the following fact [O’D14]:

$$ \begin{split}&\text{The polynomials }\Big\{\sqrt{p(1-p)}^{-|E(H)|}\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-p)\Big\}_{H\subseteq E(K_{n})}\\
&\text{are orthonomral with respect to }\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{G}(n,p).\end{split} $$

When computationally restricted to poly-time algorithms, a tester needs to apply a poly-time computable polynomial $f.$ What are classes of poly-time computable polynomials? One such class is of sufficiently low-degree polynomials (where degree refers to the largest number of edges in a monomial corresponding to some $H$ for which $\widehat{f}(H)$ is non-zero). Since those are usually not $\{0,1\}$ -valued, one needs to threshold after computing the polynomial, which leads to the following definition, motivated by Chebyshev’s inequality.

#### Definition 8 (Success of a Low-Degree Polynomial, e.g. [Hop18]).

We say that a polynomial $f:\{0,1\}^{E(K_{n})}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}$ distinguishes $H_{0}$ and $H_{1}$ with high probability if

$$ \Big|\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim H_{0}}[f(\mathbf{G})]-\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim H_{1}}[f(\mathbf{G})]\Big|=\omega\Big(\sqrt{\mathsf{Var}_{\mathbf{G}\sim H_{0}}[f(\mathbf{G})]+\mathsf{Var}_{\mathbf{G}\sim H_{1}}[f(\mathbf{G})]}\Big). $$

If $f$ is poly-time computable, this leads to the poly-time algorithm which compares $f(\mathbf{G})$ to $\big(\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim H_{0}}[f(\mathbf{G})]+\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim H_{1}}[f(\mathbf{G})]\big)/2.$

Very commonly, one takes $f$ to be a signed subgraph count [BDER14]. That is, for some small graph $A$ (e.g. triangle or wedge), one computes

$$ \mathsf{SC}^{p}_{A}(\mathbf{G}):=\sum_{H\subseteq K_{n}\;:H\sim A}\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{H}(\mathbf{G}), $$

where $H\sim A$ denotes graph isomorphism. I.e., one computes the total number of signed weights.

Importantly, the framework of [Hop18] allows one to refute the existence of low-degree polynomials which distinguish with high probability $H_{0}$ and $H_{1}.$ Namely, the condition in Definition 8 fails for all low-degree polynomials. Of course, one needs to quantify “low-degree”. Typically, this means degree $O(\log n).$ While not all $O(\log n)$ -degree polynomials are necessarily poly-time computable, the class of $O(\log n)$ -degree polynomials captures a broad class of algorithms including subgraph counting algorithms [Hop18], spectral algorithms [BKW19], SQ algorithms (subject to certain conditions) [BBH+21a], approximate message passing algorithms (with constant number of rounds) [MW22], and are in general conjectured to capture all poly-time algorithms for statistical tasks in sufficiently noisy high-dimensional regimes [Hop18].

#### Definition 9 (Low-Degree Polynomial Hardness).

We say that no low-degree polynomial distinguishes $H_{0}$ and $H_{1}$ with probability $\Omega(1)$ if there exists some $D=\omega(\log n)$ such that

$$ \Big|\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim H_{0}}[f(\mathbf{G})]-\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim H_{1}}[f(\mathbf{G})]\Big|=o\Big(\sqrt{\mathsf{Var}_{\mathbf{G}\sim H_{0}}[f(\mathbf{G})]+\mathsf{Var}_{\mathbf{G}\sim H_{1}}[f(\mathbf{G})]}\Big) $$

holds for all polynomials of degree at most $D.$ In particular, this holds (see [KVWX23], for example), if $\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim H_{1}}[f(\mathbf{G})]/\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim H_{0}}[f(\mathbf{G})^{2}]-1=o_{n}(1)$ for all polynomials $f$ of degree at most $D.$

Using the orthonormality in Eq. 16, this condition simplifies significantly when $H_{0}=\mathsf{G}(N,p)\odot\mathcal{M}$ for some mask $\mathcal{M}.$ 22 2 This fact holds and usually stated for general binary distributions when $H_{0}$ is a product distribution [Hop18], but we only state the result in the case of interest. Recall the notation in Eq. 1.

#### Claim 3.1 ([Hop18]).

Suppose that $H_{0}=\mathsf{G}(N,p)\odot\mathcal{M},H_{1}=\mathsf{R}\odot\mathcal{M}$ and $D=\omega(\log n).$ If

$$ \sum_{H\subseteq E(\mathcal{M})\;:\;1\leq|E(H)|\leq D}\Big(\Phi^{p}_{\mathsf{R}}(H)\Big)^{2}=o_{n}(1), $$

no low-degree polynomial can distinguish $H_{0}$ and $H_{1}$ with probability $\Omega(1).$

For our results on the planted coloring, we need a more sophisticated version of Claim 3.1 due to [KVWX23] when $H_{0}=\mathsf{PCol}.$ We phrase and prove a variant of it in Proposition 6.3. When applying Claim 3.1 and variations of it, we will frequently reduce calculations to the following inequality. It is similar to [KVWX23, Proposition 4.9].

#### Proposition 3.1.

For any absolute constant $\theta>0$ and $D=O((\log n)^{1.1}),$

$$ \sum_{H\in\mathcal{G}_{D}}n^{-\theta|V(H)|}=o_{n}(1). $$

#### Proof.

When $v=|V(H)|\leq D^{2/3},$ the number of graphs on $v$ vertices is at most $2^{\binom{v}{2}}\leq 2^{v^{2}}\leq 2^{vD^{2/3}}=2^{o_{n}(|V(H)|\log n)}.$ On the other hand, when $v=|V(H)|\geq D^{2/3},$ the number of graphs on $v$ vertices and at most $D$ edges is at most $\sum_{j=1}^{D}\binom{\binom{v}{2}}{D}\leq D\Big(\frac{2v^{2}}{D}\Big)^{D}\leq 2^{4D\log v}.$ As $D=(\log n)^{1.1},$ $v\geq D^{2/3},$ one has $4D\log v=4v(D\log v)/v=o_{n}(v\log n)=o_{n}(|V(H)|\log n).$ In either case, the number of graphs on $v$ vertices and at most $D$ edges is $2^{o_{n}(|V(H)|\log n)},$ which for large enough $n$ is at most $e^{\frac{\theta}{2}|V(H)|\log n}.$ Hence, for large enough $n,$

$$ \sum_{H\in\mathcal{G}_{D}}e^{-\theta|V(H)|\log n}\leq\sum_{v=1}^{2D}e^{-\frac{\theta}{2}v\log n}=O(Dn^{-\theta/4})=o_{n}(1), $$

as desired. We used the fact that a graph induced by $D$ edges has at most $2D$ vertices. ∎

### 3.3 Signed Expectations of Graphs with Leaves

Graphs with leaves are special to the current work as they separate ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}$ and ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}.$ In the spherical case, one can prove the following fact.

#### Proposition 3.2.

Suppose that $H$ is graph with a leaf $u$ which has neighbour $v.$ Suppose further that $(f_{ji})_{(ji)\in E(H)}:[-1,1]\longrightarrow[0,1]$ are some measurable functions. Then,

$$ \displaystyle\E_{V_{1},V_{2},\ldots,V_{n}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}f_{ji}(\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle)\Big] \displaystyle=\E_{\{V_{i}\}_{i\neq u}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)\backslash\{(uv)\}}f_{ji}(\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle)\Big]\times\E_{V_{u},V_{v}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[f_{uv}(\langle V_{u},V_{v}\rangle)\Big]. $$

In particular, if $H$ is a tree,

$$ \E_{V_{1},V_{2},\ldots,V_{n}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}f_{ji}(\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle)\Big]=\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}\E_{V_{i},V_{j}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[f_{ji}(\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle)\Big]. $$

#### Proof.

This follows immediately from the following homogeneity property of ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}:$

$$ \text{For every fixed $v_{j}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1},$ }\langle v_{j},V_{i}\rangle\text{ has the same distribution}. $$

Hence,

$$ \begin{split}&\E_{V_{1},V_{2},\ldots,V_{n}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}f_{ji}(\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle)\Big|\Big]\\
&=\E_{\{V_{i}\}_{i\neq u}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\E_{V_{u}\sim\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}f_{ji}(\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle)\Big|\{V_{i}\}_{i\neq u}\Big]\Big]\\
&=\E_{\{V_{i}\}_{i\neq u}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)\backslash\{(uv)\}}f_{ji}(\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle)\E_{V_{u}\sim\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[f_{uv}(\langle V_{u},V_{v}\rangle)\Big|V_{v}\Big]\Big]\\
&=\E_{\{V_{i}\}_{i\neq u}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)\backslash\{(uv)\}}f_{ji}(\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle)\E_{V_{u},V^{\prime}_{v}\sim\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[f_{uv}(\langle V_{u},V^{\prime}_{v}\rangle)\Big|V_{v}\Big]\Big]\\
&=\E_{\{V_{i}\}_{i\neq u}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)\backslash\{(uv)\}}f_{ji}(\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle)\Big]\times\E_{V_{u},V_{v}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[f_{uv}(\langle V_{u},V_{v}\rangle)\Big],\end{split} $$

where $V^{\prime}$ is some independent copy of $V^{\prime}_{v}.$ ∎

For $f_{ji}(x)=\mathds{1}[x\geq\tau^{p}_{d}]-p,$ this shows that signed expectations of graphs with leaves vanish with respect to ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}.$ It turns out that this is not true for Gaussian geometric graphs. Namely, one can show the following statement.

#### Lemma 3.2 (Lower Bound on Signed Expectation of Wedges).

Consider the wedge on 3 vertices $1,2,3$ with edges $(21),(31).$ Then, if $p\leq 0.49,$

$$ \E_{\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}}\Big[(G_{21}-p)(G_{31}-p)\Big]\geq\frac{p^{2}}{{d}}(\log d)^{-4}. $$

The proof of this fact is simple. It follows by conditioning on the norms $\|Z_{i}\|_{2}$ of Gaussian vectors. This reduces the problem to a spherical random geometric graph in which, however, the thresholds are dependent on the values $\|Z_{i}\|_{2}$ and, in particular, not equal to $\tau^{p}_{d}$ (or $\rho^{p}_{d}$ ). Nevertheless, we can still use the factorization property of the spherical random geometric graphs Proposition 3.2. We carry out the calculation in Section A.4.

The following decomposition will also be useful when studying Gaussian random geometric graphs and spherical against the planted coloring (in the planted coloring setting, note that signed weights are not orthonormal for the null distribution $\mathsf{PCol}(n,q),$ hence we need to consider a different basis and, thus, also graphs with leaves might have non-trivial expectations in this basis).

#### Definition 10 (Leaf Decomposition).

For a graph $H,$ decompose its edges into two parts – a tree part $\mathsf{TP}(H)$ and no-leaves part $\mathsf{NLP}(H)$ as follows. Initially, let $H_{0}=H.$ While $H_{0}$ has a leaf $u,$ find its neighbor $v,$ add the edge $(uv)$ to $\mathsf{TP}(H),$ and remove the edge $(uv)$ from $H_{0}.$ At the end, $\mathsf{NLP}(H)=E(H)\backslash\mathsf{TP}(H).$

#### Observation 3.3.

The following claims hold for the leaf decomposition.

- 1. $\mathsf{TP}(H)$ is a forest and $\mathsf{NLP}(H)$ has minimal degree 2 in each connected component.

- 2. If $H$ has no acyclic connected component, $|V(H)|=|V(\mathsf{NLP}(H))|+|E(\mathsf{TP}(H))|.$

We obtain a mild and easy improvement of Theorem 1.1 which, however, will be useful when discussing the edge-query model for Gaussian random geometric graphs. We prove it in Section A.6.

#### Proposition 3.3.

Suppose that (A) holds and $H$ is connected. Then, there exists some absolute constant $C$ depending only on $\epsilon,\gamma$ in (A) such that for $\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}$ and $\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)},$

$$ \Big|\E\Big[\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(G_{ji}-p)\Big]\Big|\leq(8p)^{|E(H)|}\times\Big(\frac{C\times|V(H)|\times|E(H)|\times(\log d)^{2}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)^{|E(\mathsf{TP}(H))|+\mathsf{OEI}(\mathsf{NLP}(H))}. $$

#### Remark 9.

This inequality would follow directly from an improvement of Theorem 1.1 to $\mathsf{SOEI}(H)$ as one can show that $\mathsf{SOEI}(H)\geq|E(\mathsf{TP}(H))|+\mathsf{SOEI}(\mathsf{NLP}(H)).$ Indeed, this follows from the following observation. Let $\pi^{\prime}$ be in $\arg\max_{\sigma}\mathsf{SOEI}_{\sigma}(H)$ over permutations of $[|V(\mathsf{NLP}(H))|].$ Extend $\pi^{\prime}$ to $\pi$ by assigning the numbers $\{|V(\mathsf{NLP}(H))|+1,|V(\mathsf{NLP}(H))|+2,\ldots,|V(H)|\}$ to the rest of the vertices in decreasing order as in the leaf-processing step of the definition of $\mathsf{TP}(H).$

### 3.4 Probability

The bounds in this section are all elementary and aim to rigorously quantify the following heuristic. Consider $Z_{1},Z_{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}).$ Then, $\langle Z_{1},Z_{2}\rangle$ is approximately distributed as $\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}).$ The rapid decay of Gaussian tails suggests that the density of $\langle Z_{1},Z_{2}\rangle$ around $\rho^{p}_{d}$ (recall that $\rho^{p}_{d}$ is defined by $p=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[\langle Z_{1},Z_{2}\rangle\geq\rho^{p}_{d}]$ ) is roughly $p\sqrt{d}.$ Hence, for any “short” interval $[\rho^{p}_{d}+a,\rho^{p}_{d}+a+\Delta]$ of length $\Delta$ sufficiently close to $\rho^{p}_{d},$ it must be the case that $\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[\langle Z_{1},Z_{2}\rangle\in[\rho^{p}_{d}+a,\rho^{p}_{d}+a+\Delta]]\approx p\sqrt{d}\Delta.$ Bounds of this form (where $\langle Z_{1},Z_{2}\rangle$ is replaced by $\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d})$ or $\langle V_{1},V_{2}\rangle$ for $V_{1},V_{2}\sim\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$ will be frequently used throughout.

An impatient reader is welcome to read the statements of 3.4, 3.6 and 3.5 and continue to the much more conceptually interesting Section 2.

#### 1. Gaussian Random Variables.

We use normalized Gaussian random variables $\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}).$ The density of $X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d})$ is given by $\phi_{d}(x):=\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp(-dx^{2}/2).$ We record several simple facts about Gaussians, all of which follow immediately from the following elementary proposition.

#### Proposition 3.4 (Folklore).

If $x>0$ and $Y\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1),$ $\Big(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{x^{3}}\Big)\frac{e^{-x^{2}/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\leq\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[Y\geq x]\leq\frac{1}{x}\frac{e^{-x^{2}/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}.$

#### Fact 3.4.

For $X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}),$ the following hold:

- 1. $\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[X\geq t]\leq\exp(-t^{2}d/2)$ for $t\geq\sqrt{1/d}.$

- 2. If $\xi^{p}_{d}$ is such that $\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[X\geq\xi_{d}^{p}]=p$ for some $p,d$ under (A), then $\frac{0.1\sqrt{\log(1/p)}-10}{\sqrt{d}}\leq\xi_{d}^{p}\leq\frac{\sqrt{2\log(1/p)}}{\sqrt{d}}.$

- 3. Under (A), $\phi_{d}(\xi^{p}_{d})\leq C^{\prime}pd\xi^{p}_{d}\leq C^{\prime}p\sqrt{\log d}\sqrt{d}$ for some constant $C^{\prime}.$

- 4. Suppose that (A) holds $a\in\mathbb{R},\Delta\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ are such that $|a|,|\Delta|\leq(\log d)^{-1}/\sqrt{d}.$ Then, for some absolute constant $C^{\prime\prime}>0,$

$$ {\Delta p}{\sqrt{d}}/(C^{\prime\prime}\sqrt{\log d})\leq\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}\Big[X\in[\xi^{p}_{d}+a,\xi^{p}_{d}+a+\Delta]\Big]\leq{\Delta p}{\sqrt{d}}\times(C^{\prime\prime}\sqrt{\log d}). $$

#### Proof.

1. Follows from setting $x=t\sqrt{d}$ in Proposition 3.4. 2. Again, this holds from Proposition 3.4. For the upper bound, it is enough to show that $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\log(1/p)}}\frac{e^{-\log(1/p)}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}<p,$ which is trivial. For the lower bound, there is nothing to prove if $0.1\sqrt{\log(1/p)}\leq 10.$ Otherwise, we can prove the stronger inequality $\sqrt{\log(1/p)}/\sqrt{d}\leq\xi^{p}_{d}.$ Indeed,

$$ \displaystyle\Big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log(1/p)}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log(1/p)}^{3}}\Big)e^{-\sqrt{\log(1/p)}^{2}/2}\geq\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\log(1/p)}}\sqrt{p}\geq p. $$

3. This follows from 2 for the following reason. Consider the density at $\xi^{p}_{d}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\sqrt{(\log d)}}.$ Then,

$$ \displaystyle p\geq\int^{\xi^{p}_{d}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\sqrt{(\log d)}}}_{\xi^{p}_{d}}\phi_{d}(t)dt\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\sqrt{(\log d)}}\phi_{d}(\xi^{p}_{d}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\sqrt{(\log d)}}) \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\sqrt{(\log d)}}\phi_{d}(\xi^{p}_{d})\times\exp\Big(-d\big(\xi^{p}_{d}\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\sqrt{(\log d)}}+\frac{1}{2d(\log d)}\big)\Big), $$

which immediately gives the first inequality. Using the bounds on $\xi^{p}_{d}$ from 2., we bound the last expression above and obtain $p\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}\sqrt{(\log d)}}\phi_{d}(\xi^{p}_{d})C^{\prime\prime}$ which gives the second inequality. 4. Part 1 implies that for some constant $\eta$ depending only on $\gamma,\epsilon$ in (A), $\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[X\in[\xi^{p}_{d},\xi^{p}_{d}+\frac{\eta\sqrt{\log d}}{\sqrt{d}}]]\geq p/2.$ On the other hand, whenever $|\xi^{p}_{d}-u|\leq\frac{(\log d)^{-1}}{\sqrt{d}},$ then $\phi_{d}(\xi^{p}_{d})/\phi_{d}(u)=\exp(-d((\xi^{p}_{d}-u)\xi^{p}_{d}-(\xi^{p}_{d}-u)^{2}/2))\in[1/C^{\prime\prime\prime},C^{\prime\prime\prime}]$ for some absolute constant $C^{\prime\prime\prime}$ under (A) as $|\xi^{p}_{d}|\times|\xi^{p}_{d}-u|=o(1/d),(\xi^{p}_{d}-u)^{2}=o(1/d)$ by 2. Combining these statements, at least a $\Omega(\Delta\sqrt{d}/\sqrt{(\log d)})$ fraction of the $p/2$ mass is in $[\xi^{p}_{d}+a,\xi^{p}_{d}+a+\Delta]$ which immiediately gives the lower bound as the density in this interval is $\Omega(\phi_{d}(\xi^{p}_{d})).$ Similarly, at most a $O(\Delta\sqrt{d}\sqrt{(\log d)})$ fraction of the $p/2$ mass is in $[\xi^{p}_{d}+a,\xi^{p}_{d}+a+\Delta]$ which gives the upper bound. ∎

#### 2. $\chi^{2}$ Random Variables.

The $\chi^{2}(d)$ distribution is the distribution of $\sum_{i=1}^{d}X_{i}^{2},$ where $X_{1},\ldots,X_{i}\sim_{iid}\mathcal{N}(0,1).$ We will need the following proposition.

#### Proposition 3.5 ([LM00]).

If $Z\sim\chi^{2}(d),$ then $|\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[|Z/d-1|\geq t]|\leq 2\exp(-dt^{2}/16)$ for all $t\leq 1.$

#### 3. Thresholds.

Finally, we will prove bounds on the values $\rho^{p}_{d},\tau^{p}_{d}$ from Definition 1.

#### Proposition 3.6.

Under (A), $|\tau^{p}_{d}-\xi^{p}_{d}|\leq\frac{(\log d)^{2}}{d}$ and $|\rho^{p}_{d}-\xi^{p}_{d}|\leq\frac{(\log d)^{2}}{d}.$

#### Proof.

We begin with $\rho^{p}_{d}.$ Let $Z_{1},Z_{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}).$ By Eq. 2, $\langle Z_{1},Z_{2}\rangle=Z_{11}Z_{21},$ where $dZ^{2}_{11}\sim\chi^{2}(d),Z_{21}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ are independent. Hence,

$$ \displaystyle p=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[\langle Z_{1},Z_{2}\rangle\geq\rho^{p}_{d}]=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[Z_{11}Z_{21}\geq\rho^{p}_{d}] \displaystyle\geq\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}\Big[Z_{21}\geq\frac{\rho^{p}_{d}}{1-(\log d)/\sqrt{d}}\Big]-\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}[Z_{11}\leq 1-(\log d)/\sqrt{d}] \displaystyle\geq\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}\Big[Z_{21}\geq\frac{\rho^{p}_{d}}{1-(\log d)/\sqrt{d}}\Big]-\exp(-\Omega((\log^{2}d))). $$

Hence, $\rho^{p}_{d}/(1-(\log d)/\sqrt{d})\leq\xi^{p}_{d}+\frac{1}{d}$ by part 4 of Fact 3.4 applied to $\xi^{p}_{d}+a=\rho^{p}_{d},\xi^{p}_{d}+a+\Delta=\rho^{p}_{d}/(1-(\log d)/\sqrt{d}).$ Similarly, $\rho^{p}_{d}(1+(\log d)/\sqrt{d})\geq\xi^{p}_{d}-\frac{1}{d}.$ The argument for $\tau^{p}_{d}$ is the same except that one argues about $\langle Z_{1},Z_{2}\rangle/(\|Z_{1}\|_{2}\|Z_{2}\|_{2}=Z_{21}/\|Z_{2}\|_{2}.$ ∎

Combining with the 4-th fact in Fact 3.4, we obtain:

#### Corollary 3.5.

Let $X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}).$ Suppose that (A) holds $a\in\mathbb{R},\Delta\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ are such that $|a|,|\Delta|\leq(\log d)^{-1}/\sqrt{d}.$ Then, for some absolute constant $C^{\prime\prime}>0,$

$$ {\Delta p}{\sqrt{d}}/(C^{\prime\prime}\sqrt{\log d})\leq\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}\Big[X\in[\tau^{p}_{d}+a,\tau^{p}_{d}+a+\Delta]\Big]\leq{\Delta p}{\sqrt{d}}\times(C^{\prime\prime}\sqrt{\log d}), $$

$$ {\Delta p}{\sqrt{d}}/(C^{\prime\prime}\sqrt{\log d})\leq\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}\Big[X\in[\rho^{p}_{d}+a,\rho^{p}_{d}+a+\Delta]\Big]\leq{\Delta p}{\sqrt{d}}\times(C^{\prime\prime}\sqrt{\log d}), $$

#### Corollary 3.6.

Suppose that (A) holds $a\in\mathbb{R},b\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ are such that $|a|,|\Delta|\leq(\log d)^{-1}/\sqrt{d}.$ Then, for some absolute constant $C^{\prime\prime}>0,$

$$ \displaystyle{\Delta p}{\sqrt{d}}/(C^{\prime\prime}\sqrt{\log d})-e^{-C^{\prime\prime}(\log d)^{2}}\leq\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}_{V_{1},V_{2}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\langle V_{1},V_{2}\rangle\in[\tau^{p}_{d}+a,\tau^{p}_{d}+a+\Delta]\Big]\leq \displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\leq{\Delta p}{\sqrt{d}}\times(C^{\prime\prime}\sqrt{\log d})+e^{-C^{\prime\prime}(\log d)^{2}}, \displaystyle{\Delta p}{\sqrt{d}}/(C^{\prime\prime}\sqrt{\log d})-e^{-C^{\prime\prime}(\log d)^{2}}\leq\,{\rm I}\kern-1.79993pt{\rm P}_{Z_{1},Z_{2}\sim_{iid}\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d})}\Big[\langle Z_{1},Z_{2}\rangle\in[\rho^{p}_{d}+a,\rho^{p}_{d}+a+\Delta]\Big]\leq \displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\leq{\Delta p}{\sqrt{d}}\times(C^{\prime\prime}\sqrt{\log d})+e^{-C^{\prime\prime}(\log d)^{2}}. $$

#### Proof.

The proofs in the Gaussian and spherical settings are essentially the same. In the Gaussian case, we write $\langle Z_{1},Z_{2}\rangle=Z_{11}Z_{21}.$ Then, we condition on $Z_{11}\in 1\pm(\log d)/\sqrt{d}$ as in Proposition 3.6 which happens with probability $1-\exp(-\Omega((\log d)^{2})).$ Then, we are in the setting of Corollary 3.5 with a value of $\Delta$ changed by a multiplicative factor of $1\pm O(\log d/\sqrt{d}).$ We apply Corollary 3.5. ∎

## 4 Distinguishing Spherical RGG and Erdős-Rényi

#### Proof of Theorem 1.5.

Suppose that $d\geq(M^{1/2}p)^{3+c}$ for some constant $c>0.$ Let $D=(\log n)^{1.1}$ and $\mathbf{G}_{0}\sim\mathsf{G}(N,p),\mathbf{G}_{1}\sim\mathsf{RGG}(N,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p).$ In light of Claim 3.1, we simply need to show that

$$ \sum_{H\subseteq E(\mathcal{M})\;:\;1\leq|E(H)|\leq D}\Big(\Phi^{p}_{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}(H)\Big)^{2}=o_{n}(1). $$

Note that each isomorphic copy of $H$ has the same Fourier coefficient under the ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}$ distribution. Hence, if $N(H,\mathcal{M})$ denotes the number of subgraphs of $\mathcal{M},$ this is equivalent to

$$ \sum_{H\in\mathcal{G}_{D}}N(H,\mathcal{M})\Big(\Phi^{p}_{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}(H)\Big)^{2}=o_{n}(1). $$

A beautiful result in [Alo81] shows that $N(H,\mathcal{M})\leq C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}M^{(|V(H)|+\delta(H))/2}$ for all $H$ and $M$ -vertex graphs $\mathcal{M},$ where $C$ is some absolute constant.33 3 [Alo81] explicitly only shows that $N(H,\mathcal{M})\leq C_{H}M^{(|V(H)|+\delta(H))/2}$ where $C_{H}$ is some constant depending only on $H.$ However, one can easily track in the argument this constant to be $|V(H)|^{O(|V(H)|)}$ which is enough. In fact, Alon shows that this result is tight up to the choice of constant $C_{H}.$

By Proposition 3.2, it is enough to consider the case when $H$ has no leaves.

Now, we will use Theorems 1.1 and 1.2. Observe that for $H$ connected, $\mathsf{OEI}(H)\geq\frac{1}{3}(2\lceil\frac{|V(H)|-1}{2}\rceil+\delta(H)+1)\geq\frac{|V(H)|+\delta(H)}{3}.$ However, as all of $\mathsf{OEI}(H),|V(H)|,\delta(H)$ are obviously additive over disjoint unions, the inequality $\mathsf{OEI}(H)\geq\frac{|V(H)|+\delta(H)}{3}$ holds for disconnected $H$ as well. We obtain:

$$ \begin{split}&\sum_{H\in\mathcal{NLG}_{D}}N(H,\mathcal{M})\Big(\Phi^{p}_{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}(H)\Big)^{2}\\
&\leq\sum_{H\in\mathcal{NLG}_{D}}C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}M^{(|V(H)|+\delta(H))/2}\times\Big(\Big(8\sqrt{\frac{p}{1-p}})^{|E(H)|}\Big(\frac{(\log n)^{4}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)^{\mathsf{OEI}(H)}\Big)^{2}\\
&\leq\sum_{H\in\mathcal{NLG}_{D}}C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}128^{|E(H)|}p^{|E(H)|}M^{(|V(H)|+\delta(H))/2}\times\Big(\frac{(\log n)^{8}}{d}\Big)^{(|V(H)|+\delta(H))/3}.\end{split} $$

Now, we use the following proposition.

#### Proposition 4.1.

Suppose that $H$ is a graph without isolated vertices and leaves. Then, $|E(H)|\geq|V(H)|+\delta(H).$

#### Proof.

Note that in a graph $H$ without isolated vertices and leaves, each vertex has degree at least $2.$ By Proposition 2.1, there exists some independent set $S$ such that $|S|-|N_{H}(S)|=\delta(H)$ and, hence, $S\cap N_{H}(S)=\emptyset.$ In particular, this means that among the vertices $A=S\cup N_{H}(S),$ there are at least $2|S|$ edges with both endpoints in $A$ (as each vertex in $S$ has at least two neighbours and both are in $N_{H}(S)$ by definition of $N_{H}(\cdot)$ ). On the other hand, each vertex in $V(H)\backslash A$ is also adjacent to at least two edges, so there are at least $\frac{1}{2}\times 2(|V(H)|-|A|)$ more edges. Altogether, this means that the number of edges in $H$ is at least

$$ 2|S|+(|V(H)|-|A|)=2|S|+|V(H)|-|S|-|N_{H}(S)|=|V(H)|+|S|-|N_{H}(S)|=|V(H)|+\delta(H), $$

as desired. ∎

Going back to Eq. 22, we bound

$$ \begin{split}&\sum_{H\in\mathcal{NLG}_{D}}C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}128^{|E(H)|}p^{|E(H)|}M^{(|V(H)|+\delta(H))/2}\times\Big(\frac{(\log n)^{8}}{d}\Big)^{(|V(H)|+\delta(H))/3}\\
&\leq\sum_{H\in\mathcal{NLG}_{D}}C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}128^{|E(H)|}p^{|V(H)|+\delta(H)}M^{(|V(H)|+\delta(H))/2}\times\Big(\frac{(\log n)^{8}}{d}\Big)^{(|V(H)|+\delta(H))/3}\\
&=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{NLG}_{D}}C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}128^{|E(H)|}\Big(\frac{M^{1/2}p(\log n)^{8}}{d^{1/3}}\Big)^{(|V(H)|+\delta(H))}\\
\end{split} $$

As $d\geq(M^{1/2}p)^{3+c},$ under (A), $\Big(\frac{M^{1/2}p(\log n)^{8}}{d^{1/3}}\Big)\leq n^{-\theta}$ for some constant $\theta>0$ (depending only on $\delta,\gamma$ from (A), and $c$ from Theorem 1.5). Recall that $M=\Theta(n^{2}).$ Also, $\delta(H)\geq 0$ (by taking $S=V(H)$ in the definition). Hence, we can bound Eq. 23 by

$$ \begin{split}&\sum_{H\in\mathcal{NLG}_{D}}C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}128^{|E(H)|}\Big(\frac{M^{1/2}p(\log n)^{8}}{d^{1/3}}\Big)^{(|V(H)|+\delta(H))}\\
&\leq\sum_{H\in\mathcal{NLG}_{D}}C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}128^{|E(H)|}n^{-|V(H)|\theta}=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{NLG}_{D}}C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}128^{|E(H)|}e^{-|V(H)|\theta\log n}.\end{split} $$

Note that $|V(H)|\leq 2|E(H)|\leq 2D=O((\log n)^{1.1}).$ Thus, $|V(H)|^{1.1}=o_{n}(|V(H)|\log n).$ Similarly, $E(H)\leq\min(|V(H)|^{2},D)\leq|V(H)|D^{1/2}=o_{n}(|V(H)|\log n).$ Hence, for all large enough $n,$ the expression above is bounded by

$$ \sum_{H\in\mathcal{NLG}_{D}}e^{-\frac{\theta}{2}|V(H)|\log n}. $$

The last expression is bounded by $\sum_{H\in\mathcal{G}_{D}}e^{-\frac{\theta}{2}|V(H)|\log n}$ which is enough by Proposition 3.1. ∎

## 5 Distinguishing Gaussian RGG and Erdős-Rényi

### 5.1 Proof of Theorem 1.6

#### 5.1.1 Detection Lower Bound

Suppose that $d\geq\max(n^{3/2}p)^{1+c},(n^{3}p^{3})^{1+c}).$ We will prove that no degree $D=(\log n)^{1.1}$ polynomial distinguishes the two graph models. We proceed as in Section 4 with $\mathcal{M}=K_{n}.$ Using the obvious bound $N(K_{n},H)\leq n^{|V(H)|}$ (as one can choose each of the $|V(H)|$ labeled vertices of $H$ in at most $n$ ways), we need to show the following analogue of Eq. 21.

$$ \sum_{H\in\mathcal{G}_{D}}n^{|V(H)|}\Big(\Phi^{p}_{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}(H)\Big)^{2}=o_{n}(1). $$

Now, consider any graph $H$ on $v$ vertices and $e$ edges. Suppose that its connected components are $H_{1},H_{2},\ldots,H_{r},$ where $H_{i}$ has $v_{i}$ vertices and $e_{i}$ edges. Clearly, $\sum_{i=1}^{r}e_{i}=e,\sum_{i=1}^{r}v_{i}=v$ and $\Phi^{p}_{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}(H)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\Phi^{p}_{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}(H_{i}).$ Clearly, if any of the graphs $H_{i}$ is a single edge, $\Phi^{p}_{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}(H_{i})=0,$ so we can focus on the case $e_{i}\geq 2,v_{i}\geq 3$ $\forall i.$ Now, suppose that $H_{1},H_{2},\ldots,H_{t}$ are trees and $H_{t+1},H_{t+2},\ldots,H_{r}$ are not. Then, using Proposition 3.3,

- 1. For $1\leq u\leq r,$ $\displaystyle\Big|\Phi^{p}_{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}(H_{i})\Big|=\Big|\Big(\sqrt{\frac{1}{p(1-p)}}\Big)^{e_{i}}\E[\prod_{(uv)\in E(H_{i})}(G_{uv}-p)]\Big|$ $\displaystyle\leq\Big(\sqrt{\frac{1}{p(1-p)}}\Big)^{e_{i}}\Big(\frac{p(\log n)^{4}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)^{e_{i}}\leq\Big(\frac{2p(\log n)^{8}}{d}\Big)^{v_{i}/3}.$ We used $e_{i}=v_{i}-1\geq 2v_{i}/3$ twice.

- 2. For $r+1\leq u\leq t,$ $\displaystyle\Big|\Phi^{p}_{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}(H_{i})\Big|=\Big|\Big(\sqrt{\frac{1}{p(1-p)}}\Big)^{e_{i}}\E[\prod_{(uv)\in E(H_{i})}(G_{uv}-p)]\Big|$ $\displaystyle\leq\Big(\sqrt{\frac{1}{p(1-p)}}\Big)^{e_{i}}p^{e_{i}}\times\Big(\frac{(\log n)^{4}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)^{\lceil(v_{i}-1)/2\rceil}\leq(2\sqrt{p})^{e_{i}}\Big(\frac{(\log n)^{4}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)^{v_{i}/3}\leq\Big(\frac{8p^{3}(\log n)^{4}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)^{v_{i}/3}.$ This time, we used $v_{i}\geq e_{i}$ (as $H_{i}$ is connected and not a tree) and $\lceil(v_{i}-1)/2\rceil\geq v_{i}/3.$

Altogether, this means that

$$ \Big|\Phi^{p}_{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}(H)\Big|\leq\Big(\frac{2p(\log n)^{8}}{d}\Big)^{\sum_{i=1}^{r}v_{i}/3}\times\Big(\frac{8p^{3/2}(\log n)^{4}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)^{\sum_{i=r+1}^{t}v_{i}/3}. $$

Hence, as $|V(H)|=\sum_{i=1}^{t}v_{i},$

$$ n^{|V(H)|}\Phi^{p}_{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}(H)^{2}\leq\Big(\frac{2p(\log n)^{8}n^{3/2}}{d}\Big)^{\sum_{i=1}^{r}2v_{i}/3}\times\Big(\frac{8p^{3}n^{3}(\log n)^{4}}{{d}}\Big)^{\sum_{i=r+1}^{t}v_{i}/3}. $$

As $d\geq(n^{3/2}p)^{1+c},d\geq(n^{3}p^{3})^{1+c}$ and (A) holds, this last expression is clearly at most $n^{-\theta|V(H)|}$ for some absolute constant $\theta$ depending only on $\epsilon,\gamma$ from (A) and $c$ from Theorem 1.7. The claim follows from Proposition 3.1.

#### 5.1.2 Detection Algorithms

#### 1. Detecting via signed wedges.

We want to show that if $d=o\Big((n^{3/2}p)(\log n)^{-4}\Big),p\leq 0.49$ and (A) holds, the signed wedge count statistic distinguishes ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}$ and $\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ with high probability in the sense of Definition 8. The condition $p<0.49$ is needed as ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},\frac{1}{2})}$ and ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),\frac{1}{2})}$ are the same distribution.

Recall the definition of signed counts Eq. 17. By Lemma 3.2,

$$ \E_{\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}}[\mathsf{CS}^{p}_{\wedge}(\mathbf{G})]=n\binom{n-1}{2}\E[\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{\wedge(1,2,3)}(\mathbf{G})]\geq\frac{n^{3}p^{2}}{4d}\times(\log d)^{-4}. $$

Clearly, $\E_{\mathbf{H}\sim\mathsf{\mathbf{G}}(n,p)}[\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{\wedge}(\mathbf{H})]=0.$ Now, we compute the variances. Note that, with respect to either distribution,

$$ \mathsf{Var}\Big[\mathsf{CS}^{p}_{\wedge}\Big]=\sum_{(i,j,k)}\mathsf{Var}[\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{\wedge(i,j,k)}]+\sum_{\wedge(i,j,k)\neq\wedge(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})}\mathsf{Cov}[\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{\wedge(i,j,k)},\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{\wedge(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})}]. $$

Importantly, observe that for any two labelled subgraphs $H_{1},H_{2},$ one has $\mathsf{Cov}[\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{H_{1}},\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{H_{2}}]=\E[\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{H_{1}}\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{H_{2}}]-\E[\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{H_{1}}]\E[\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{H_{2}}].$ However,

$$ \begin{split}&\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{H_{1}}(G)\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{H_{2}}(G)\\
&=\prod_{e_{1}\in E(H_{1})}(G_{e_{1}}-p)\times\prod_{e_{2}\in E(H_{2})}(G_{e_{2}}-p)\\
&=\prod_{e\in E(H_{1})\triangle E(H_{2})}(G_{e}-p)\times\prod_{e\in E(H_{1})\cap E(H_{2})}(G_{e}-p)^{2}\\
&=\prod_{e\in E(H_{1})\triangle E(H_{2})}(G_{e}-p)\times\prod_{e\in E(H_{1})\cap E(H_{2})}((G_{e}-p)(1-2p)+(p-p^{2}))\\
&=\sum_{A\subseteq E(H_{1})\cap E(H_{2})}\prod_{e\in(E(H_{1})\triangle E(H_{2}))\cup A}(G_{e}-p)(1-2p)^{|A|}(p-p^{2})^{|E(H_{1})\cap E(H_{2})|-|A|}.\end{split} $$

In particular, the covariance is also easily expressed as a linear combination of signed weights (which should be no surprise as any polynomial can be expanded in the Fourier basis). The above expression immediately shows that unless $H_{1}=H_{2},$ the covariance with respect to $\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ is 0 as an edge in $E(H_{1})\triangle E(H_{2})$ has expectation $0.$ When $H_{1}=H_{2}=\wedge(i,j,k),$ the covariance is bounded by $p^{|E(H)|}=p^{2}.$ Hence, $\mathsf{Var}_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{G}(n,p)}\Big[\mathsf{CS}^{p}_{\wedge}(\mathbf{G})\Big]=O(n^{3}p^{2})$ For the geometric distribution, we can use Proposition 3.3 to bound the covariance. We carry out this trivial calculation in Section A.1 and show that $\mathsf{Var}_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{RGG}}\Big[\mathsf{CS}^{p}_{\wedge}(\mathbf{G})\Big]=o\Big((\log d)^{8}\times\Big(n^{3}p^{2}+n^{5}p^{4}/d^{2}+n^{4}p^{3}/d+n^{4}p^{4}/d^{2}\Big)\Big),$ which is enough to conclude by Definition 8.

#### 2. Detecting via signed triangles.

We want to show that if $d=o\Big((n^{3}p^{3})(\log n)^{-1}\Big)$ for some absolute constant $c$ and (A) holds, the signed triangle count statistic distinguishes ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}$ and $\mathsf{G}(n,p).$ The proof is analogous to the ones given in [BDER14, LMSY22], but we give it for completeness. We will use the following claim, the proof of which is presented in Section A.5.

#### Lemma 5.1.

$\displaystyle\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}}\Big[\mathsf{SW}^{p}_{\triangle}(\mathbf{G})\Big]\geq\frac{Cp^{3}(\log d)^{-1}}{\sqrt{d}}$ for some absolute constant $C.$

As in the proof for wedges, we know that $\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}}[\mathsf{CS}^{p}_{\triangle}(\mathbf{G})]\geq\frac{Cn^{3}p^{3}(\log d)^{-1}}{6\sqrt{d}},$ $\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{G}(n,p)}[\mathsf{CS}^{p}_{\triangle}(\mathbf{G})]=0,\mathsf{Var}_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{G}(n,p)}[\mathsf{CS}^{p}_{\triangle}(\mathbf{G})]=\Theta(n^{3}p^{3}).$ In Section A.2 we show that $\mathsf{Var}_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{RGG}}[\mathsf{CS}^{p}_{\triangle}(\mathbf{G})]=O\Big(n^{5}p^{6}(\log d)^{4}/d+n^{4}p^{5}(\log d)^{4}/d+n^{3}p^{3}\Big),$ which is enough.

### 5.2 Proof of Theorem 1.7

#### 5.2.1 Detection Lower Bounds

Suppose that $d\geq\max\Big((Mp)^{1+c},(M^{3/2}p^{3})^{1+c}\Big).$ We want to show that for all $\mathcal{M}$ on $M$ edges and $N$ vertices, the distributions $\mathbf{G}_{0}\sim\mathsf{G}(N,p)\odot\mathcal{M},\mathbf{G}_{1}\sim\mathsf{RGG}(N,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)$ are indistinguishable with respect to low degree polynomials. As in Section 4, we simply need to show that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{H\in\mathcal{G}_{D}}C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}\times M^{(|V(H)|+\delta(H))/2}\times\Big(\Phi^{p}_{{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}}(H)\Big)^{2}=o_{n}(1). $$

Decompose $H$ into $\mathsf{TP}(H)$ and $\mathsf{NLP}(H)$ as in Definition 10. Let $\mathsf{TP}(H)$ be composed of trees $T_{1},T_{2},\ldots,T_{k}.$ We will use the following claim.

#### Proposition 5.1.

Let $H$ be a graph. Suppose that there exist two graphs $H_{1},H_{2}$ such that $|V(H_{1})\cap V(H_{2})|\leq 1$ and $E(H)=E(H_{1})\cup E(H_{2}).$ Then,

$$ |V(H)|+\delta(H)\leq(|V(H_{1})|+\delta(H_{1}))+(|V(H_{2})|+\delta(H_{2})). $$

#### Proof.

If $|V(H_{1})\cap V(H_{2})|=0,$ this claim is trivial as both $|V(H)|$ and $\delta(H)$ are additive over disjoint unions. Suppose that $V(H_{1})\cap V(H_{2})=\{a\}.$ Let $S\in\arg\max_{S^{\prime}\subseteq V(H)}|S^{\prime}|-|N_{H}(S^{\prime})|.$ Let $S_{1}=S\cap V(H_{1}),S_{2}=S\cap V(H_{2}).$ It is enough to show that

$$ \displaystyle|V(H)|+|S|-|N_{H}(S)|\leq|V(H_{1})|+|S_{1}|-|N_{H_{1}}(S_{1})|+|V(H_{2})|+|S_{2}|-|N_{H_{2}}(S_{2})|\;\Longleftrightarrow \displaystyle|S|+|N_{H_{1}}(S_{1})|+|N_{H_{2}}(S_{2})|\leq|S_{1}|+|S_{2}|+|N_{H}(S_{1}\cup S_{2})|+1. $$

Now, observe that $|S|\leq|S_{1}|+|S_{2}|$ trivially. However, $|N_{H_{1}}(S_{1})|+|N_{H_{2}}(S_{2})|\leq|N_{H}(S_{1}\cup S_{2})|+1.$ Indeed, this holds as $N_{H_{1}}(S_{1})\cup N_{H_{2}}(S_{2})\subseteq N_{H}(S_{1}\cup S_{2})$ and $N_{H_{1}}(S_{1})\cap N_{H_{2}}(S_{2})\subseteq\{a\}.$ ∎

As each tree $T_{i}$ has at most one common vertex with $\mathsf{NLP}(H)$ and none with other trees, we apply the above lemma inductively and obtain

$$ |V(H)|+\delta(H)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}(|V(T_{i})|+\delta(T_{i}))+|V(\mathsf{NLP}(H))|+\delta(\mathsf{NLP}(H)). $$

Using Proposition 3.3, we bound Eq. 26 as follows.

$$ \begin{split}&\sum_{H\in\mathcal{G}_{D}}C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}\times M^{(|V(H)|+\delta(H))/2}\times p^{|E(H)|}\Big(\frac{(\log n)^{10}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)^{2|E(\mathsf{TP}(H))|+2\mathsf{OEI}(\mathsf{NLP}(H))}\\
&\leq\sum_{H\in\mathcal{G}_{D}}C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}\times M^{\sum_{i=1}^{k}(|V(T_{i})|+\delta(T_{i}))/2+(|V(\mathsf{NLP}(H))|+\delta(\mathsf{NLP}(H)))/2}\\
&\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\times p^{\sum_{i=1}^{t}|E(T_{i})|+|E(\mathsf{NLP}(H))|}\Big(\frac{(\log n)^{10}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)^{2\sum_{i=1}^{t}|E(T_{i})|+2\mathsf{OEI}(\mathsf{NLP}(H))}.\end{split} $$

Now, we use the following simple combinatorial claim.

#### Claim 5.2.

For any non-empty tree $T,$ $\delta(T)\leq|V(T)|-2.$

#### Proof.

Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that $\delta(T)\geq|V(T)|-1.$ As in Proposition 2.1, there exists some independent set $S$ such that $\delta(T)=|S|-|N_{T}(S)|.$ Hence, $|S|\geq|V(T)|-1.$ As $T$ is connected, $|N_{T}(S)|\geq 1.$ As $S$ is independent, $S\subseteq V(T)\backslash N_{T}(S),$ so $|S|\leq|V(T)|-1.$ Altogether, $\delta(T)=|S|-|N_{T}(S)|\leq|V(T)|-2,$ contradiction. ∎

We also use $V(\mathsf{NLP}(H))+\delta(\mathsf{NLP}(H))\leq|E(H)|$ from Proposition 4.1 as $\mathsf{NLP}(H)$ has minimal degree $2$ and $\mathsf{OEI}(H)\geq\frac{|V(\mathsf{NLP}(H))|+\delta(H)}{3}$ from Proposition 1.2.

Combining these, we bound the last expression by

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{H\in\mathcal{G}_{D}}C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}\times M^{\sum_{i=1}^{k}(|V(T_{i})|-1)+(|V(\mathsf{NLP}(H))|+\delta(\mathsf{NLP}(H)))/2}\times \displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad p^{\sum_{i=1}^{t}|E(T_{i})|+|E(H)|}\Big(\frac{(\log n)^{10}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)^{2\sum_{i=1}^{t}|E(T_{i})|+2\frac{|V(\mathsf{NLP}(H))|+\delta(H)}{3}} \displaystyle\leq\sum_{H\in\mathcal{G}_{D}}C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}\times M^{\sum_{i=1}^{k}|E(T_{i})|+(|V(\mathsf{NLP}(H))|+\delta(\mathsf{NLP}(H)))/2}\times \displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad p^{\sum_{i=1}^{t}|E(T_{i})|+(|V(\mathsf{NLP}(H))|+\delta(\mathsf{NLP}(H)))}\Big(\frac{(\log n)^{10}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)^{2\sum_{i=1}^{t}|E(T_{i})|+2\frac{|V(\mathsf{NLP}(H))|+\delta(H)}{3}} \displaystyle\leq\sum_{H\in\mathcal{G}_{D}}C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}\times\prod_{i=1}^{t}\Big(\frac{Mp(\log n)^{20}}{d}\Big)^{|E(T_{i})|}\times\Big(\frac{M^{3/2}p^{3}(\log n)^{20}}{d}\Big)^{(|V(\mathsf{NLP}(H))|+\delta(H))/3}. $$

Now, whenever $d\geq\max\Big((Mp)^{1+c},(M^{3/2}p^{3})^{1+c}\Big),$ this last expression is bounded by $n^{-\theta|V(H)|}$ for some absolute constant $\theta$ under $\eqref{eq:assumption}.$ As $|V(H)|=O(D)=O((\log n)^{1.1}),$ the entire expression is bounded by

$$ \sum_{H\in\mathcal{G}_{D}}C^{|V(H)|^{1.1}}n^{-\theta|V(H)|}\leq\sum_{H\in\mathcal{G}_{D}}n^{-\theta|V(H)|/2}=o_{n}(1), $$

the last following from Proposition 3.1.

#### 5.2.2 Detection Algorithm

To detect with sample complexity $M=d(\log d)^{17}/p,$ choose a mask $\mathcal{M}$ which is the union of $A=(\log n)^{17}$ disjoint stars on $N=d$ leaves. Then, $M=AN=(Np)(\log d)^{17}$ Observe that all subgraphs are stars and the number of $\mathsf{Star}_{k}$ subgraphs is $A\times\binom{N}{k}=\Theta(AN^{k})$ for $k$ constant.

By Lemma 3.2, the expect signed count of wedges is

$$ \E_{\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}}[\mathsf{CS}_{\wedge}]=\Theta\Big(AN^{2}\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}}[\mathsf{SW}_{\wedge(1,2,3)(\mathbf{G})}]\Big)=\Omega(AN^{2}p^{2}(\log d)^{-4}/d). $$

The expectation with respect to $\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ is clearly 0 and the variance $\Theta(AN^{2}p^{2}).$ As in the unmasked case, we analyze the variance with respect to ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}$ in Section A.3 based on the overlap patterns and show that it is of order $O\Big(AN^{4}p^{4}(\log d)^{8}/d^{2}+AN^{3}p^{3}(\log n)^{4}/d+AN^{2}p^{2}\Big)$ which is enough for the condition in Definition 8 to hold.

## 6 RGG versus Planted Coloring

Our first step is to choose $q$ appropriately. We do this in such a way that the “most informative” triangle Fourier coefficients of $\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},1/2)$ and $\mathsf{PCol}(n,q)$ (nearly) match.

After that, we follow nearly explicitly the method of [KVWX23] for proving low-degree indistinguishability to $\mathsf{PCol}(n,q).$ It is based on a clever analysis of the bound in Definition 9 exploiting the ambient Erdős-Rényi structure of $\mathsf{PCol}(n,q).$ As a large part of the analysis is nearly identical to [KVWX23], we delay many of the proofs to Appendix B.

### 6.1 Choice of $q$

From Theorem 1.1 and [BDER14, Lemma 1], it immediately follows that $\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},1/2)}[\mathsf{SW}_{\triangle}(\mathbf{G})]\in\Big[\frac{(\log d)^{-1}}{\sqrt{d}},\frac{\log d}{\sqrt{d}}\Big].$ We want to find some $q$ which leads to the same signed expectation of a triangle in $\mathsf{PCol}(n,q).$ Computing signed expectations for $\mathsf{PCol}(n,q)$ is very easy with the same strategy for computing Fourier coefficients as in the planted clique case described in Section 1.2.

#### Proposition 6.1.

Consider some graph $H$ and $\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{PCol}(n,q).$ Then,

- 1. If $H$ has a leaf, $\E[\mathsf{SW}^{1/2}_{H}(\mathbf{G})]=0.$

- 2. $\E[\mathsf{SW}^{1/2}_{\triangle}(\mathbf{G})]=\frac{1}{8q^{2}}+\frac{3}{8(q-1)q^{2}}-\frac{(q-2)}{8q^{2}(q-1)^{2}}$

- 3. $|\E[\mathsf{SW}^{1/2}_{H}]|\leq\Big(\frac{|V(H)|}{q}\Big)^{|V(H)|-|\mathsf{CC}(H)|}.$

We prove this proposition in Section B.1 and now continue to the choice of $q.$ We define $q$ by rounding some real $q_{1}$ which exactly matches the signed triangle expectation.
